title: The 4-minute Mile: Greatest Sports Story?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about intros and Charlie's Angels (Cheryl Ladd), then tell the story of the four-minute mile. They trace the mile's origins from Greek stadion and Roman miles marked by roads, through 19th-century pedestrianism and pub-run mile races, Captain Robert Barclay's sub-five-minute mile, and Walter George's 1886 "Mile of the Century." They cover the record progression (Norman Tabor, Paavo Nurmi, Jules Ladoumègue, Jack Lovelock, Glenn Cunningham, Gunder Hägg and Arne Andersson), and Brutus Hamilton's claim that the mile was physiologically impossible. The main story is Roger Bannister: his Oxford training as a medical student, his 1952 Helsinki Olympic fourth-place finish, his physiology research with Norris McWhirter, his pacers Chris Chataway and Chris Brasher, and his 3:59.4 run on May 6, 1954 at Iffley Road. Also covered: John Landy breaking the record weeks later, the 1954 Miracle Mile against Landy, the modern record holders, and Dick Fosbury as a teaser for a future episode. The episode closes with a listener mail about the TV show Brains Gone Wild and the sign-off.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about intros, Charlie's Angels and Cheryl Ladd, and Josh says the episode idea came from the HBO show Winning Time.

segments.title: Origins of the mile and foot racing
segments.summary: The hosts trace running from the Greek stadion and the Romans' mille passus through Roman roads and English servant races, and then to the British definition of the mile in statute.

segments.title: Pedestrianism and the 19th-century mile
segments.summary: Running was called pedestrianism and raced around pubs and taverns. Quarter-mile tracks were built around sporting fields. Captain Robert Barclay became the first to break five minutes.

segments.title: Gentleman amateurs and Walter George's Mile of the Century
segments.summary: Amateur gentlemen runners looked down on professionals. Walter George ran 4:12 in 1886 against William Cummings in front of about 20,000 spectators at Lillie Bridge, and the hosts discuss how close this came to four minutes.

segments.title: Record progression and Glenn Cunningham
segments.summary: The record fell gradually through Norman Tabor, Paavo Nurmi, Jules Ladoumègue, Jack Lovelock, and Glenn Cunningham, whose childhood burn injury is recounted. Track was popular in the US then, and the hosts speculate on its decline.

segments.title: Hägg and Andersson and the belief the four-minute mile was impossible
segments.summary: Swedes Gunder Hägg and Arne Andersson traded the record, with Hägg reaching 4:01.4 in Malmö, about four strides short of four minutes. Brutus Hamilton's published limits argued the mile was physiologically impossible.

segments.title: Roger Bannister's training, studies and Helsinki
segments.summary: Bannister trained while studying medicine at Oxford without a coach. He researched running physiology, worked with Norris McWhirter as a test subject, and aimed for the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, where he finished fourth in the 1500 meters. He then set his sights on the four-minute mile.

segments.title: The May 6, 1954 four-minute mile
segments.summary: Bannister planned pacing with Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway at Iffley Road in Oxford despite rainy weather, after a false start. He ran 3:59.4, the first sub-four-minute mile, announced by Norris McWhirter.
topics: pacers Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway

segments.title: Aftermath, Landy, Miracle Mile and current records
segments.summary: John Landy broke the record weeks later, and in 1954 Bannister and Landy both broke four minutes at the Vancouver Miracle Mile. The hosts note the number of sub-four-minute runners, the current records (El Guerrouj and Hassan), and tease a future Dick Fosbury episode.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break and transition back to content.

segments.title: Listener mail on Brains Gone Wild
segments.summary: A listener writes about the TV show Brains Gone Wild on Discovery Plus and says he has caught up on the podcast.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and invite accolades by email.
